title: Distributed Email Service (Gmail-style)
problem: Design a distributed email service like Gmail supporting SMTP send/receive, spam filtering, full-text search, and attachments.
summary: A hybrid write + read system where email is ingested over SMTP (inbound MX + outbound MTA), filtered for spam/malware, split into metadata (indexed, searchable) and body/attachment blobs (cheap storage), and surfaced to clients over HTTP/IMAP. The dominant design choice is separating metadata from message bodies: metadata lives in a sharded SQL/NoSQL store with a secondary search index, while bodies land in a KV message store and attachments in a blob store (content-addressed to dedupe). The main tradeoff is eventual consistency between the metadata DB and the search index — users might send a mail that isn't searchable for a few seconds. Sized for ~1B users and ~200B messages/day (Gmail scale).

functional: Accept inbound SMTP on port 25 and apply spam, virus, and DMARC checks
Send outbound mail to peer MTAs with retry on 4xx temporary failures
Store messages split by metadata, body, and attachments; lazy-load bodies
Expose HTTP and IMAP APIs for list, fetch, search, label, and delete
Full-text search across subject, body, and attachment text within ~5 s freshness
Push new-mail notifications to connected clients in real time
nonFunctional: Support 1B DAU and 200B messages/day with ~115K write QPS and ~460K read QPS
Durability: no accepted message is ever lost, stored in at least three replicas
Attachment upload resumable up to 25 MB per file
Search index staleness under 5 s at p99

assumptions: 1B DAU, 10 sends + 40 receives per user per day
Average email 50 KB text, 10% carry attachments averaging 500 KB
Spam rate ~50% at the MX edge (most dropped pre-filter, ~10% reach inbox filter)
estimates: Attachment storage: 200B * 0.1 * 500KB ≈ 10 PB/day raw, ~3 PB after content-addressed dedupe

client.name: Client (Web / Mobile / IMAP)
client.summary: Gmail web app, mobile app, or IMAP client that composes, lists, and searches mail.

sections.heading: Protocols
sections.body:
- HTTPS REST/gRPC for first-party web and mobile
- IMAP/SMTP for third-party clients (Outlook, Apple Mail)
- Long-poll or WebSocket for new-mail push

sections.heading: Composition
sections.body: Client drafts locally, auto-saves every 30s, then POSTs MIME-encoded message to `/v1/messages:send`. Attachments are uploaded separately via signed URL and referenced by content hash.

sections.heading: Inbox view
sections.body: List endpoint returns metadata only (sender, subject, snippet, flags). Body is lazy-fetched on open. This keeps the inbox-list call under 50ms even with thousands of messages.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Email is the classic split-read pattern: users scroll metadata 100x more often than they open bodies, so the metadata path must be blazing fast.

bottlenecks.title: Inbox list payload bloat on cold load
bottlenecks.trigger: User with years of mail opens the app; client requests /v1/messages?labelIds=INBOX&maxResults=50 but also syncs labels, threads, and unread counters. At 40 receives/user/day * 365d = ~14.6K messages/year, metadata-only responses can still exceed several MB if snippets aren't trimmed.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cold inbox load exceeds the 50ms target, spinner lingers 2–5s on mobile/slow networks, users perceive Gmail as 'slow to open'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Strict server-side snippet cap (~150 chars), pagination with maxResults=50 + cursor, HTTP/2 + gzip/brotli on responses, and an on-device IndexedDB cache keyed by (user_id, history_id) so subsequent loads are delta-syncs only.
bottlenecks.detection: Client RUM metric: p95 time-to-first-inbox-row and response payload size histogram; alert when p95 payload > 500KB or TTFR > 1s.

bottlenecks.title: Attachment upload stalls on flaky mobile links
bottlenecks.trigger: User attaches a file near the 25MB MIME cap over a 3G/spotty LTE connection; single PUT to signed URL must complete before send can proceed. At 10% attachment rate * 500KB avg but tail up to 25MB, worst-case uploads take 30s+.
bottlenecks.symptom: Compose window appears hung; user hits Send again, creating duplicate drafts; battery drain from TCP retries; eventual upload failure forces full retry from byte 0.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Resumable uploads (RFC-style chunked PUT with Content-Range, à la GCS resumable or tus.io), 5–10MB chunks, client-side SHA-256 computed in a Web Worker so Content-Addressed dedup short-circuits re-uploads of already-stored blobs.
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry: upload_bytes_sent vs upload_bytes_acked, retry count per attachment; alert when p95 upload-retry-ratio > 1.5 or abandonment rate > 2%.

bottlenecks.title: Push/WebSocket fan-in connection limits
bottlenecks.trigger: Long-lived WebSocket per client for real-time new-mail push. At 1B DAU with multiple devices each, a single web app tab reconnects on every network flap; aggressive reconnect storms after a regional blip can overwhelm the client's own event loop and drain mobile battery.
bottlenecks.symptom: Missed new-mail notifications, UI shows stale unread counts until manual refresh, mobile OS kills background socket, users complain 'mail only arrives when I open the app'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Fall back to APNs/FCM on mobile (no persistent socket), exponential backoff with jitter (base 1s, cap 60s) for web-push reconnects, and a history-id resync on reconnect so any missed events replay from the metadata CDC cursor rather than being lost.
bottlenecks.detection: Client-reported reconnect_rate and notification_gap_seconds metrics; alert when median reconnects/hour > 5 per session or when history-id gap on resync > 50 messages.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the client is called out as its own component In most system-design diagrams the client is just "the thing that calls the API" — barely worth discussing. For Gmail-style email, the client is genuinely load-bearing, because email has two quirks that force real logic onto the device: **users scroll metadata ~100× more than they open bodies**, and **the protocol surface isn't just HTTPS — it's also IMAP and SMTP** for third-party apps like Outlook and Apple Mail. If the client were dumb, every inbox scroll would drag full message bodies across the network, and the whole IMAP ecosystem would be locked out. ### What breaks without a smart client Imagine no local cache and no lazy body-fetch. Every time Bob opens Gmail, the server ships him thousands of full MIME messages. The metadata DB gets hammered with redundant reads, the body KV serves 50 KB blobs that nobody reads past the subject line, and the inbox-list p95 blows past the 50ms target. On a flaky mobile link, a half-sent 25 MB attachment means the user hits Send again and creates a duplicate draft — because there's no resumable-upload logic on the device. ### The number that makes this obvious Peak read traffic is **~1.4M QPS** (1B users × 40 receives/day ÷ 86400, with peak factor). If each inbox open pulled full bodies at 50 KB average, that's 1.4M × 50 KB = **70 GB/sec** of egress — versus ~1.5 GB/sec if the client asks only for metadata + 150-char snippets. The client's lazy-fetch discipline is what makes the read path affordable. ### The trade-off Pushing logic onto the client (IndexedDB cache, delta-sync via history-id, chunked uploads) means more client code to maintain and keep consistent across Web, iOS, Android, and IMAP — but the server savings are worth it at this scale.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer for the mail submission API tier.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: Only web/mobile API traffic. Inbound SMTP (port 25) hits a separate L4 LB in front of the MX receiver.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Least-connections with health-check ejection after 3 consecutive 5xx in 10s. TLS terminated here; plaintext HTTP to the API inside the VPC.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: Multi-AZ HA pair; anycast VIP so a single AZ outage is invisible to clients.

bottlenecks.title: TLS handshake CPU exhaustion at peak send+read fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: Combined API traffic peaks at ~350K send QPS + ~1.4M read QPS ≈ 1.75M HTTPS req/s. Mobile clients reconnect frequently (cell handoffs, app foregrounding), and without session resumption each new TCP connection forces a full ECDHE+RSA/ECDSA handshake at ~2–5ms of CPU per core per handshake.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegs at 90%+, p99 connect latency balloons from <5ms to 200ms+, clients see TLS handshake timeouts and spinner on app open; on-call sees cascading 5xx as health checks themselves start failing.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT where safe, aggressive session ticket + session ID resumption (24h TTL), ECDSA P-256 certs instead of RSA-2048 (3–5x cheaper handshakes), dedicated TLS-terminating hardware/NIC offload (e.g., Intel QAT), and HTTP/2 connection coalescing so one conn serves many requests per client.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB `ssl_handshakes_per_sec` vs `ssl_resumption_ratio` (target >80% resumed); CPU per LB node >70%; p99 `ssl_handshake_time_ms` >20ms.

bottlenecks.title: Connection concurrency ceiling vs. configured capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: Sim config lists concurrency=50000 per LB; with 1.4M peak read QPS and WebSocket/long-poll connections held open for new-mail push (1B DAU * multi-device), concurrent open sockets easily exceed 50K per node. A single-AZ failure halves fleet capacity, doubling per-node load.
bottlenecks.symptom: New connections get SYN-dropped or queued behind `somaxconn`; clients see 'connection refused' or 30s+ connect stalls; WebSocket reconnect storms amplify the problem after any blip.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Separate the WebSocket/push tier onto its own LB pool (don't mix with short-lived REST), raise `net.core.somaxconn` and `nofile` ulimits, enable connection draining on deploys, and autoscale on active-connection count (not just CPU) with 2x headroom for AZ-failure absorption.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-node `active_connections` gauge with alert at 70% of configured max; `listen_overflows` and `tcp_abort_on_memory` counters; SYN backlog drops in kernel netstat.

bottlenecks.title: Slow-upstream head-of-line blocking from attachment uploads
bottlenecks.trigger: Attachment uploads up to 25MB over slow mobile links can tie up an LB→API connection for 30+ seconds. At 10% of 115K send QPS = ~11.5K concurrent uploads peak, a single LB node with 50K concurrency can see 20%+ of its slots stuck on slow uploads, starving fast metadata reads.
bottlenecks.symptom: Inbox list p95 latency spikes to seconds even though API replicas are idle; LB shows high concurrency but low request rate; users report 'Gmail is slow' while attachment senders see normal behavior.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route `/v1/attachments:upload` to a dedicated LB listener/backend pool with its own concurrency budget, enforce per-connection idle and total-duration timeouts (e.g., 60s idle, 300s total), and push clients to upload directly to blob store via signed URL (bypassing the LB entirely for bytes).
bottlenecks.detection: Per-route p99 latency and active-connection histograms; alert when `/attachments` route consumes >25% of LB connection slots or when inbox-list p95 diverges from API backend p95 by >100ms.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why there's a load balancer in front of the Mail Submission API For a Gmail-style service handling **~1.4M peak read QPS** and **~350K peak send QPS**, no single API server can absorb that traffic — you need roughly 100 stateless API replicas to spread the load. The load balancer is what makes those 100 boxes *look* like one endpoint (`mail.googleapis.com`) to every web and mobile client. It also terminates TLS centrally, so API replicas don't each burn CPU on handshakes, and it ejects unhealthy replicas within seconds so a crashed box doesn't become a black hole for inbox loads. Note that this LB only handles HTTPS API traffic. Inbound SMTP on port 25 hits a *separate* L4 LB in front of the MX receivers — SMTP is a different protocol with different failure semantics, so mixing them behind one device would be a mess. ### What happens without it Point DNS directly at one API box and that box instantly melts at peak. Point DNS at all 100 boxes via round-robin DNS and you get a different disaster: when one replica crashes, roughly 1% of users get connection refused for the ~5 minutes until DNS TTLs expire, and clients have no way to route around it. Operators see a flood of 5xx; the metadata DB sees uneven load because DNS can't rebalance based on actual replica health. ### The number that forces it At 1.4M peak read QPS spread across 100 replicas, that's **14K req/sec per replica** — tight but workable. Lose the LB and lose health-based routing, and even a single bad replica (1% of fleet) is 14K failed requests/sec hitting real users' inboxes. ### The trade-off The LB becomes a critical path dependency, so it must be run as a multi-AZ HA pair with an anycast VIP — extra operational surface in exchange for a single stable entry point.

api.name: Mail Submission API
api.summary: Stateless service handling send, list, read, search, and attachment upload coordination.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
POST /v1/messages:send # submit a new message
GET /v1/messages?labelIds=INBOX&maxResults=50
GET /v1/messages/{id} # full MIME body
GET /v1/messages:search?q=...
POST /v1/attachments:upload # returns signed URL
```

sections.heading: Send path
sections.body:
1. Parse and validate MIME (size limit 25 MB, RFC 5322 headers)
2. Persist attachments by content hash (dedupe) to blob store
3. Write body to message KV, metadata to inbox DB
4. Route: if recipient domain == local (gmail.com) → deliver to inbox pipeline; else → hand to outbound MTA
5. Return 202 Accepted with message id

sections.heading: Auth
sections.body: OAuth2 bearer token for HTTP; SASL PLAIN over TLS for SMTP submission on port 587.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless → scale on CPU. At peak ~350K send QPS and ~15ms service time, ~5K concurrent reqs/replica → ~100 replicas.

bottlenecks.title: MIME parsing CPU saturation at peak send QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak ~350K send QPS each requiring full RFC 5322 parse, header validation, address normalization, and 25MB size enforcement. With ~100 replicas that's 3.5K sends/sec/replica, and a single 25MB message with deeply nested multipart boundaries can burn 50–200ms of CPU on the parser alone — 5–40x the 5–20ms service budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 send latency climbs from ~20ms to 500ms+, CPU pegged at 95% across the fleet, 202 Accepted responses slow down, LB starts marking replicas unhealthy under load, compose UI shows 'sending...' for seconds and users double-send.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hard-cap parser recursion depth and boundary count (reject > 100 parts or > 10 nesting levels with 400), stream-parse with a bounded buffer rather than loading full 25MB into memory, offload large-message parsing to a dedicated replica pool via a size-based route (> 1MB → 'heavy' pool), and use a native-code MIME parser (e.g., mailparse in Rust via FFI) instead of pure-Python/JS.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-replica CPU% and `mime_parse_duration_ms` histogram tagged by message_size_bucket; alert when p99 parse time > 100ms or when CPU > 80% sustained 5min. Track `mime_parse_rejections_total` by reason (depth, size, malformed).

bottlenecks.title: Thundering-herd fan-out on multi-recipient sends blocking the 202
bottlenecks.trigger: Send path does body KV write + metadata insert + attachment refcount before returning 202. A mailing-list send to 500 internal gmail.com recipients fans out to 500 body KV writes + 500 metadata inserts + N attachment incref calls — at 5–15ms per KV op serially that's 2.5–7.5 seconds, far beyond any reasonable API timeout.
bottlenecks.symptom: Bulk-send requests hit the 30s LB timeout and return 504, client retries create duplicate deliveries for the first half of recipients, metadata DB sees write amplification spikes, and one noisy sender can saturate a single API replica's 3000 concurrency slots.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Return 202 after only the sender's Sent-folder write + enqueue to an internal fan-out queue (Kafka/PubSub); downstream workers do per-recipient body+metadata writes asynchronously with idempotency keyed on (message_id, recipient). Batch KV writes in groups of 50 via multi-key API. Enforce max 500 recipients per request (RFC 5321 already allows rejecting).
bottlenecks.detection: Per-request `recipient_count` histogram and `send_fanout_duration_ms` tagged by recipient-count bucket; alert when any request holds an API slot > 2s or when a single user_id consumes > 5% of concurrency slots for 1min.

bottlenecks.title: Attachment verification HEAD storm against blob store
bottlenecks.trigger: Every send with attachments issues a blob.exists HEAD per attachment reference before accepting. At peak 115K send QPS with 10% carrying attachments averaging 1–3 references each, that's ~15–35K HEAD calls/sec to the blob tier on the hot path. A blob-store latency blip (p99 60ms → 300ms) directly stalls the send path.
bottlenecks.symptom: Send p95 tracks blob-store p95 rather than the 15ms API target; intermittent 502s during blob-store GC or rebalance events; API replicas pile up in `wait-on-blob-HEAD` state and exhaust the 3000 concurrency budget.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache attachment-exists results in a replica-local LRU (TTL 5min, keyed by sha256) since upload-then-send happens within seconds; issue HEADs in parallel with `asyncio.gather`/goroutines rather than serially; trust the signed-URL upload receipt (which already proves existence) and skip HEAD when the client presents a fresh upload token < 10min old.
bottlenecks.detection: `attachment_head_latency_ms` p99 and `attachment_head_cache_hit_ratio` gauges; alert when cache-hit < 70% or when HEAD p99 > 50ms, and on correlation between send-latency spikes and blob-HEAD latency spikes.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the Mail Submission API exists here Gmail has to accept mail from two completely different worlds: modern web/mobile clients that speak HTTPS, and the entire SMTP ecosystem (third-party apps, other mail servers). The Mail Submission API is the **orchestrator** that turns a raw send request into all the correct side effects: MIME parsing, 25 MB size enforcement, attachment dedup lookup, body write, metadata write, spam hand-off, and routing to either the local inbox pipeline or the outbound MTA. Without a single coordinating service, every client would need to know about every backing store — and every backing store would need to implement auth, validation, and rate-limiting. ### What breaks without it Suppose the client wrote directly to the metadata DB, body KV, and blob store. Alice hits Send; her web app writes metadata but crashes before the body write — now her Sent folder shows a ghost row pointing at a missing body. Operators see orphaned refs piling up; the spam filter is bypassed entirely, so outbound abuse goes straight to the MTA and gets Gmail's IP range blacklisted within hours. Auth logic is duplicated in four places and drifts. ### The number that forces it Peak send traffic is **~350K QPS** (1B users × 10 sends/day, peak factor). At a ~15ms service time per send, that's 350,000 × 0.015 = **5,250 concurrent requests** in flight. Split across stateless replicas at ~3K concurrency each, you need roughly **100 API replicas** — which is only possible because the service holds no state and can be scaled on CPU alone. ### Trade-off Every send now pays one extra network hop through the API tier, in exchange for a single chokepoint where validation, auth, and spam routing are enforced consistently.

spam.name: Spam / Anti-abuse Filter
spam.summary: Pipeline that scores every inbound and outbound message for spam, phish, malware.

sections.heading: Signals
sections.body:
- SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication
- Sender reputation (IP, domain)
- Bayesian + neural content classifier (Postini-style stack)
- URL scan against Safe Browsing / VirusTotal feeds
- Attachment sandbox (detonate suspicious PDFs/scripts)

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.body: Each message gets a spam score 0.0–1.0 and a disposition: INBOX, SPAM, QUARANTINE, or REJECT. Inbound rejects return SMTP 550 to the sending server.

sections.heading: Latency budget
sections.body: 50–150ms typical. Hard SLA: 500ms p99 — otherwise sending MTAs time out the SMTP DATA command.

sections.heading: Why this is its own service
sections.body: Spam rules change hourly. Pulling them into a separate tier lets the security team ship without touching the API path.

gained: No in-house ML pipeline to run
lost: Per-message cost adds up at scale

bottlenecks.title: SMTP DATA timeout from attachment sandbox detonation
bottlenecks.trigger: Hard 500ms p99 SLA per scan, but the pipeline includes attachment sandbox detonation (PDFs/scripts) plus Safe Browsing URL lookups. At ~460K inbound msgs/sec peak with 10% carrying attachments (~46K/sec needing sandbox), even a small fraction routed to full VM detonation (seconds to minutes) saturates the sandbox pool and blocks the synchronous scan call.
bottlenecks.symptom: Remote sending MTAs time out the SMTP DATA command (>2min) and retry, causing duplicate deliveries; our MX returns 451 temp-fail and queues back up; spam filter p99 climbs from 150ms to >1s; on-call sees sandbox worker queue depth alerts and inbound backlog growing on the MX tier.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Two-tier scanning: synchronous fast-path (reputation + Bayesian + URL hash lookup) under 150ms returns a provisional disposition; suspicious attachments go to an async sandbox queue and the message is held in a QUARANTINE label until detonation completes (with a 30s async budget before defaulting to SPAM). Cap synchronous path at 300ms with a hard timeout and fallback score.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `spam_scan_duration_ms` p99 by path (sync vs sandbox), `sandbox_queue_depth`, and `sandbox_detonation_timeout_rate`. Alert when sync p99 > 300ms for 2min, sandbox queue depth > 10K, or SMTP DATA 451 rate > 0.5%.

bottlenecks.title: Model/ruleset reload stampede causing scoring latency spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: Spam rules and classifier models change hourly (stated as the reason this is a separate service). With ~2000 concurrency per node and thousands of filter replicas serving ~460K inbound + ~115K outbound msgs/sec, a synchronous hot-reload or cold cache after model push forces every in-flight scan to wait on model load (hundreds of MB of neural weights + Bayesian tables).
bottlenecks.symptom: Every hour on model-push boundary, p99 scan latency spikes from 150ms to 800ms+, some nodes breach the 500ms SLA causing sending MTAs to time out, and MX receivers see a brief burst of SMTP 451 temp-fails; dashboards show synchronized latency sawtooth aligned with model-deploy timestamps.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Double-buffer model loading: load new model into a shadow slot in the background, atomically swap pointer once warm, keep old model resident for 60s grace. Stagger rollout across the fleet with a canary (1% → 10% → 100%) over 10 minutes to avoid synchronized reloads. Pre-warm classifier with a replay of last-minute traffic before swap.
bottlenecks.detection: Export `model_version_active`, `model_load_duration_ms`, and `model_swap_timestamp` per replica. Alert on p99 scan latency correlated with model_swap events, or on >5% of fleet reloading within the same 60s window.

bottlenecks.title: Per-sender reputation lookup hot keys on viral spam campaigns
bottlenecks.trigger: Reputation lookups keyed by (sender IP, sender domain) are called on every scan. During a large spam campaign, a single botnet IP or spoofed domain can hit the same reputation key at tens of thousands of QPS out of the ~460K/sec inbound — turning reputation cache/DB into a hot-shard bottleneck.
bottlenecks.symptom: Reputation store shows a single shard at 95% CPU while peers idle; scan p95 climbs for messages from the campaign's IP range; as a side-effect, legitimate senders on neighboring IPs in the same shard see elevated latency and occasional timeouts; false-negative rate rises as filter falls back to cached/stale reputation.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replica-local LRU cache (30s TTL) in front of the reputation store keyed by IP/domain — a viral campaign collapses to one backend lookup per replica per TTL. Use request coalescing (singleflight) so concurrent in-flight lookups for the same key share a single backend call. Shard reputation store by consistent hash with per-key rate limiting and hot-key replication.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `reputation_lookup_qps` by top-N keys, `reputation_cache_hit_ratio` (target >90%), and per-shard CPU skew. Alert when top-1 key exceeds 5% of total lookups or when cache hit ratio drops below 80% for 5min.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a dedicated Spam / Anti-abuse Filter sits on the critical path For a Gmail-scale service, spam isn't a nice-to-have cleanup job — it's a survival requirement. Roughly **50% of everything hitting our MX is spam**, and if any meaningful fraction of it reaches user inboxes, Gmail becomes unusable overnight. Just as bad, if *outbound* abuse slips through (compromised accounts blasting phishing), remote mail providers will blacklist Gmail's entire outbound IP range within hours, and suddenly Alice's legitimate invoice to Bob bounces. The filter has to score both directions — inbound *and* outbound — before metadata or body writes happen. ### What breaks without it Skip this tier and the inbox DB fills up with junk that nobody wants to scroll through, search relevance collapses (every `invoice` query returns 10,000 Nigerian-prince hits), and storage costs balloon — remember we're retaining mail *forever*. On the operator side, abuse reports to postmaster@ spike, major ISPs start rejecting our outbound SMTP with 550s, and the on-call sees the MTA retry queue grow unboundedly as remote servers defer our traffic. ### The number that justifies it Inbound peak is **~460K reads/sec**, but raw MX traffic is roughly **2×** that before edge drops — call it ~900K msgs/sec at peak, half of which is spam. That's ~450K spam messages/sec we must *not* write to the metadata DB. At ~1 KB metadata each, blindly accepting them would burn an extra **~40 TB/day** of DB writes and pollute the search index forever. ### The trade-off The filter adds 50–150ms to every message's path and a hard 500ms p99 SLA — real latency pressure on the send flow — in exchange for keeping inboxes clean and our sending reputation intact.

mta.name: Outbound SMTP Relay (MTA)
mta.summary: Opens SMTP connections to remote mail servers and delivers outbound messages.

sections.heading: SMTP conversation
sections.body:
```
220 mx.example.com ESMTP
EHLO gmail-smtp-out.google.com
MAIL FROM:<alice@gmail.com>
RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>
DATA... headers + body....
250 2.0.0 OK queued as 3F2504
```

sections.heading: Retry + queue
sections.body: Temporary failures (4xx) are queued; retried with exponential backoff up to 3 days (RFC 5321). After 3 days, a bounce is generated back to the sender.

sections.heading: Reputation management
sections.body: Outbound pool segmented by sender behavior: transactional / bulk / low-rep. Keeps one bad sender from blacklisting the whole IP range.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: Remote MX down → retry queue grows; remote IP-blocks our range → rotate outbound IPs and warm new range gradually.

bottlenecks.title: Retry queue explosion when major remote MX is degraded
bottlenecks.trigger: With ~115K send QPS peak and ~10% of traffic targeting any single large provider (e.g. outlook.com, yahoo.com), a 2-hour outage at that provider queues ~83M messages that must be held and retried with exponential backoff up to 3 days per RFC 5321. At 50KB avg + metadata, that's ~5TB of queued state on the MTA tier alone.
bottlenecks.symptom: Retry queue depth grows unboundedly, deferred-queue disk fills on MTA nodes, new sends compete with retries for connection slots (concurrency=1000/node), send-to-delivery latency p99 climbs from seconds to hours, and eventually 3-day expirations generate a bounce storm back to senders.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Per-destination-domain queue sharding with independent concurrency budgets (so outlook.com backlog doesn't starve example.com), circuit breaker that fast-fails retries to a degraded domain with longer backoff (min 15min between retries once >10% failure rate detected), tiered storage — move messages deferred >1h to cheap blob storage rather than holding in MTA-local disk, and per-domain queue-depth caps with shed-to-bounce at 2x normal depth.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-destination-domain gauge `mta_deferred_queue_depth{domain}` with alert at 10x baseline; `mta_retry_attempts_per_msg` histogram; `mta_disk_usage_pct` alert at 70%; track `mta_delivery_age_seconds` p99 per domain with page at >1h.

bottlenecks.title: IP reputation collapse from compromised-account blast
bottlenecks.trigger: A single compromised account or leaked OAuth token sending 10K+ phishing messages in minutes (vs. normal 10 sends/user/day) can push an outbound IP's reputation below threshold at Microsoft/Google/Yahoo within 15–30 minutes. With outbound pool IPs shared across thousands of users, one bad actor blacklists the whole range and legitimate traffic (~115K QPS) starts getting 550-rejected.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sharp spike in 550/554 permanent failures from major receivers, bounces flood back to innocent senders, Gmail appears 'broken' for outbound to specific domains, deliverability dashboards (Google Postmaster Tools, SNDS) show red, and warming a new IP range takes days during which throughput is capped.
bottlenecks.mitigation: IP pool segmentation by sender behavior tier (transactional / bulk / low-rep / new-account) as already called out — plus automated per-account rate limiting upstream at the Spam filter (hard cap e.g. 500 sends/hour for normal accounts, 50/hour for <30-day-old accounts), automatic account quarantine on anomalous burst detection (>10x baseline in 5min), and a hot-standby warm IP pool ready to promote when a primary is flagged. Enforce DKIM signing + per-domain SPF alignment so receivers can isolate the offender.
bottlenecks.detection: Real-time `mta_bounce_rate{receiver_domain}` with alert at >2% for 5min, `mta_sender_qps{user_id}` with anomaly detection at p99*10, Google Postmaster API polling for IP reputation drops, and SMTP response code distribution dashboard with paging on 550 rate >0.5%.

bottlenecks.title: Connection concurrency exhaustion on slow remote MX servers
bottlenecks.trigger: MTA node configured concurrency=1000 with serviceTimeMs up to 500ms; when a set of destinations (small corporate MX, greylisting servers) routinely take 2–10s per SMTP transaction, each connection holds a slot ~20x longer than average. With ~115K send QPS across the fleet, if 5% of destinations are slow (~5.7K QPS on slow tier) they'd need 5700 × 10s = 57K concurrent slots — exceeding fleet capacity if not isolated.
bottlenecks.symptom: MTA nodes show 90%+ concurrency utilization while CPU is idle (blocked on remote I/O), fast domains start seeing queuing delays despite being healthy, send-queue-time p95 climbs above 30s, LB marks MTA nodes unhealthy due to accept backlog.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Separate connection pools per destination-domain class (fast / slow / unknown) with independent concurrency budgets, aggressive per-connection idle timeout (30s) and total-transaction timeout (120s), HELO/EHLO + MAIL FROM pipelining to reduce round-trips, and connection reuse — keep SMTP connections open with up to 100 messages per session to amortize handshake cost for high-volume destinations.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-node `mta_active_connections` with alert at 80% of configured max, `mta_connection_duration_ms` p99 histogram tagged by destination-domain tier, and `mta_accept_queue_depth` alert at any non-zero sustained value.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the Outbound MTA is here For a Gmail-style service, the Submission API can't just "send" a message to `bob@example.com` — email delivery to external domains happens over **SMTP**, a decades-old protocol where our servers have to actually open a TCP connection to `example.com`'s mail server, negotiate TLS, and walk through a `MAIL FROM` / `RCPT TO` / `DATA` conversation. That's slow, unreliable, and full of edge cases (remote server down, greylisting, reputation blocks). You don't want that mess anywhere near the hot API path that's answering "user clicked Send." The MTA is the dedicated tier that owns this ugly, asynchronous conversation with the rest of the internet. ### What happens without it Suppose the API tried to deliver synchronously. Alice clicks Send; the API opens SMTP to a slow corporate server that takes 8 seconds to respond — Alice's browser spins for 8 seconds. Worse, if `example.com` is down, the API either fails the send (losing the message) or blocks its replica holding the request open. At 350K peak send QPS, a few thousand slow remote servers would lock up the entire API fleet within minutes. Operators would see API concurrency saturated, users would see "failed to send" on perfectly valid messages, and the retry logic required by RFC 5321 (up to 3 days!) simply wouldn't exist. ### The number that forces it Outbound peak is **~115K sends/sec**. SMTP delivery averages 50–500ms per remote, so at any instant ~115,000 × 0.3s ≈ **34,500 in-flight SMTP connections** need to exist. The API returns `202 Accepted` in ~15ms and hands off; the MTA absorbs that 34K-connection pool on its own fleet, with its own retry queue holding days of deferred mail. ### The trade-off Send acknowledgment becomes "we'll try" rather than "delivered" — the API's 202 doesn't guarantee the recipient got it, and a bounce may arrive minutes or hours later.

mx.name: Inbound MX Receiver
mx.summary: SMTP server advertised in public MX records that accepts mail from the internet.

sections.heading: Protocol
sections.body: Listens on port 25, advertises STARTTLS. Accepts MAIL FROM / RCPT TO / DATA and writes message to spam filter via internal RPC or queue.

sections.heading: Edge defenses
sections.body:
- Greylisting suspicious senders (retry → accept)
- Rate-limit per sender IP
- Early reject on invalid recipient (no user lookup required)

sections.heading: Capacity
sections.body: ~460K inbound mails/sec peak after edge-level drop of obvious spam. Scales horizontally behind an L4 anycast VIP.

bottlenecks.title: Synchronous spam-filter RPC stalls SMTP DATA ack
bottlenecks.trigger: MX must persist + get a disposition before returning 250 on DATA. At ~460K inbound msgs/sec peak (and ~900K/sec raw pre-drop), any spike in spam-filter p99 above its 500ms SLA (e.g., sandbox detonation backlog or model reload) directly blocks MX connections, each holding a slot out of the 5000-concurrency budget per node.
bottlenecks.symptom: SMTP DATA phase hangs; remote MTAs hit their own timeouts and retry, doubling inbound load; MX nodes pile up in 'waiting on scan' state, accept queue overflows, and healthy senders start seeing 451 4.7.1 temp-fails. On-call sees MX concurrency saturated while CPU is idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Decouple durability from scoring: buffer DATA to a local durable spool (fsync'd) and return 250 after spool, then run spam scan async from the spool before handing to metadata/body writers. Add a per-connection scan timeout of 300ms with fallback to deferred-scan QUARANTINE. Enforce max concurrent in-flight scans per MX node and shed with 451 before saturating.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `mx_scan_wait_ms` p99 > 300ms, `mx_active_connections` > 70% of 5000, and correlation between spam-filter p99 and MX accept-queue depth. Track SMTP 451 rate per MX node (alert > 0.2% sustained).

bottlenecks.title: Connection flood from botnet / DDoS at port 25
bottlenecks.trigger: Port 25 is publicly reachable by the entire internet. With ~50% of raw inbound being spam (~450K msgs/sec of junk at peak) and periodic botnet campaigns, a single campaign can open hundreds of thousands of concurrent SMTP connections from tens of thousands of source IPs, far exceeding the 5000-concurrency-per-node budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: MX accept queue overflows, SYN drops at the kernel, legitimate senders see 'connection refused' or long connect stalls and fall back to secondary MX (or defer for hours); greylisting logic starves under load; anycast VIP shows elevated packet loss in one region.
bottlenecks.mitigation: L4 anycast VIP with per-source-IP connection-rate limits (e.g., 10 concurrent conns/IP, 100 new conns/min/IP) enforced in the LB before reaching MX; early-reject unknown recipients before DATA (cheap user_id existence check with a bloom filter cached in-memory); aggressive greylisting for low-reputation IPs; autoscale MX replicas on active-connection count with 2x AZ-loss headroom; drop connections from IPs on public RBLs (Spamhaus) at the edge.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-source-IP connection-rate histogram, `mx_syn_backlog_drops` counter, `mx_conns_rejected_ratelimit` by reason, and `mx_active_connections` per node alert at 70% of max. Page on new-connection QPS > 3x 7-day baseline.

bottlenecks.title: Early-reject recipient lookup hot path saturating metadata DB
bottlenecks.trigger: MX performs 'early reject on invalid recipient' before DATA to avoid buffering spam for non-existent users. At ~460K inbound msgs/sec peak (and higher raw connection rate including spam probing nonexistent addresses), that's ~460K+ user-existence lookups/sec against the metadata DB or a user-directory service — potentially larger than the inbox-read path itself.
bottlenecks.symptom: User-directory / metadata DB sees a QPS spike that competes with inbox reads; MX RCPT TO latency climbs from ~10ms to 100ms+, pushing total SMTP transaction time up and reducing throughput per connection slot; directory-dictionary-attack campaigns amplify the load 10–100x.
bottlenecks.mitigation: In-memory bloom filter of all valid user_ids (1B users × ~10 bits ≈ 1.2GB per MX node) refreshed from CDC; reject definitely-missing recipients with 550 5.1.1 without hitting the DB; only confirmed-positive bloom hits do a real lookup against a read-replica user directory with replica-local LRU cache (TTL 5min). Add per-source-IP RCPT-fail rate limit to detect dictionary attacks (close connection after 5 invalid RCPTs).
bottlenecks.detection: Track `mx_recipient_lookup_qps`, `mx_recipient_bloom_hit_ratio` (target >99% for attack traffic rejected at bloom), and `mx_rcpt_invalid_per_connection` histogram. Alert when recipient-lookup QPS exceeds 2x inbound msg rate or when user-directory p99 > 20ms.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the MX Receiver is here For a Gmail-style service, the rest of the internet doesn't know about your HTTPS API — it knows how to deliver mail exactly one way: by looking up the `MX` record for `gmail.com` in DNS and opening a TCP connection to port 25 to speak SMTP. Someone has to be listening on that port, answering `220 ESMTP`, walking through `MAIL FROM` / `RCPT TO` / `DATA`, and doing it in a way that's robust against the ~50% of raw traffic that's spam, malicious, or malformed. That's the MX Receiver. It's the front door that translates "the internet's mail protocol" into "an internal message the spam filter and metadata DB can work with." ### What happens without it If there's no MX receiver, nobody outside Gmail can send mail to Gmail users — full stop. DNS lookups for `gmail.com` MX records would return nothing (or worse, point at the API load balancer, which doesn't speak SMTP and would just drop the TCP connection). Senders like `mx.acme.co` would see connection-refused errors, retry for a few days per RFC 5321, then bounce the message back to their user with "host unreachable." From Bob's perspective, his inbox just silently stops receiving anything external. ### The number Peak inbound is **~460K msgs/sec after edge-level spam drops**, from raw traffic closer to **~900K/sec**. That means the MX tier has to reject roughly **440K spam attempts/sec** at the edge — via greylisting, IP rate-limiting, and invalid-recipient rejection — before any of it touches the spam filter, metadata DB, or body store downstream. Pushing that filtering to port 25 keeps ~40 TB/day of junk writes out of the expensive tiers. ### Trade-off Running your own SMTP server on the open internet means owning a constantly-probed attack surface — in exchange for speaking the only protocol the rest of the email world understands.

meta.name: Inbox Metadata DB
meta.summary: Per-user sharded store of message metadata: headers, labels, flags, references.

sections.heading: Schema
sections.body:
```
TABLE messages user_id BIGINT (shard key) message_id UUID thread_id UUID from_addr TEXT to_addrs TEXT subject TEXT snippet TEXT labels TEXT # INBOX, STARRED, SPAM,... received_at TIMESTAMP body_ref TEXT # pointer into message body KV attach_ids TEXT # content hashes PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), received_at DESC, message_id)
```

sections.heading: Why sharded by user_id
sections.body: Inbox queries are always `WHERE user_id = X ORDER BY received_at DESC` — the natural partition key. Cassandra or Bigtable handles 73 PB spread over ~1K nodes trivially.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.body: LOCAL_QUORUM writes (RF=3). Inbox reads use LOCAL_ONE — small staleness is acceptable since a freshly sent mail also lands in the client-side optimistic cache.

gained: SQL + cross-shard transactions for label ops

bottlenecks.title: Hot-shard skew from celebrity/mailing-list recipients and power senders
bottlenecks.trigger: Partition key is user_id, but real-world fan-out is Zipfian: newsletters, support@, noreply@, and popular mailing-list aliases receive thousands of writes/sec while the median user sees <1/day. At ~460K inbound writes/sec peak, a single hot user_id can concentrate 5–20K writes/sec onto one Cassandra/Bigtable tablet, against a per-shard sustained write ceiling of ~10–20K ops/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: One shard's p99 write latency climbs from ~10ms to 200ms+ while peers are idle; compaction backlog builds on that node; LOCAL_QUORUM writes start failing with WriteTimeoutException for everyone on that shard (collateral damage to normal users co-located on it); send-path 202 latency spikes and MX spam-filter handoffs start timing out.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Sub-shard hot user_ids by appending a time-bucket or hash suffix to the partition key (e.g., `(user_id, received_at_hour_bucket)` with 16-way fan for flagged hot users); maintain a hot-user registry refreshed from write-rate telemetry; route mailing-list expansion writes through a batched async writer that coalesces 50 inserts per RPC; cap per-user write QPS at the API tier with a token bucket (e.g., 5K/sec) and shed to a slower queue above that.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-partition write-QPS and write-latency histograms (Cassandra's `org.apache.cassandra.metrics.Table.WriteLatency` tagged by token range); alert when top-1 partition exceeds 2% of cluster writes or any shard's p99 write latency > 50ms while cluster median is < 20ms; dashboard top-N user_ids by writes/min.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded per-user partition growth breaking inbox-list queries
bottlenecks.trigger: Primary key is `((user_id), received_at DESC, message_id)` with forever retention. At 40 receives + 10 sends/day = 50 msgs/day/user, a 10-year account accumulates ~180K rows in a single partition; heavy users (mailing list subscribers) hit 1M+ rows. Cassandra partitions > 100MB or > 100K rows degrade sharply on range scans and repair.
bottlenecks.symptom: Inbox-list queries (`ORDER BY received_at DESC LIMIT 50`) that should be 3–10ms creep to 50–200ms for long-tenured users; tombstone scans on deletes trigger `TombstoneOverwhelmingException`; repair and compaction on oversized partitions stall for hours; full-partition reads during node replacement time out.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Introduce a time-bucket into the partition key: `((user_id, year_month), received_at DESC, message_id)` so each partition holds ~1.5K rows; API layer queries the current + previous bucket for the default inbox view and fans out only on deep pagination. Set `gc_grace_seconds` appropriately and use TWCS (time-window compaction strategy) since data is write-once, time-ordered. Archive partitions older than N years to a cheaper cold tier keyed the same way.
bottlenecks.detection: Cassandra `MaxPartitionSize` and `MeanPartitionSize` metrics per table, alert at partition_size > 50MB or row_count > 50K; `TombstoneScannedHistogram` alert at p99 > 1000; track inbox-list p99 bucketed by user account age to catch creeping regression.

bottlenecks.title: Label/flag update write amplification on threads and bulk ops
bottlenecks.trigger: Labels are stored as a `TEXT` column on each message row; any label mutation (mark-read, star, move-to-folder, apply-filter) requires a full-row rewrite under LOCAL_QUORUM. Bulk ops (select 500 messages → archive) generate 500 rewrites; applying a new user filter retroactively can rewrite 10K+ rows. At 1B users doing ~10 label ops/day average, that's ~115K label-write QPS on top of the 460K ingestion writes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Bulk archive/delete UI actions take 5–30 seconds and occasionally time out; CDC stream to the search indexer floods with redundant updates pushing index-lag p99 past the 5s target; compaction keeps up during the day but falls behind on weekends when users do inbox cleanup; tombstone buildup on rewritten rows.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split labels into a separate narrow CQL table `message_labels(user_id, message_id, label)` with per-label rows so toggling one label is a single small insert/delete instead of a full-row rewrite; batch bulk ops into `UNLOGGED BATCH` of 50 statements per partition; for retroactive filter application use an async worker that processes in 1K-row chunks with backpressure; coalesce CDC events for the same message_id within a 1s window before emitting to the indexer.
bottlenecks.detection: Ratio of `label_update_qps / message_insert_qps` per shard (alert when > 0.5); p99 latency of the batch label-mutation endpoint; CDC backlog lag gauge > 3s for 2min; compaction pending tasks per node > 50.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the Inbox Metadata DB exists separately For a Gmail-style service, the single most common thing users do is **scroll their inbox** — they glance at sender, subject, and snippet, and only occasionally open a full message. If we stored everything (headers, body, attachments) in one big table, every inbox scroll would drag 50 KB+ of MIME body across the network just to render a one-line row. The metadata DB is the "fast lane": tiny ~1 KB rows per message, sharded by `user_id` so that Bob's inbox query (`WHERE user_id = 'bob' ORDER BY received_at DESC LIMIT 50`) is a single-partition read answered in under 10ms. Bodies and attachments live in cheaper stores and are only fetched when a user actually clicks a message. ### What happens without it Collapse metadata into the body KV and every inbox load turns into a fan-out of 50 body fetches, each 50 KB. Bob's inbox takes seconds to render on mobile; the body KV — which should be cold storage — gets hammered as if it were a hot cache. Operators see the KV's tail latency spike, search indexer lag balloons (because CDC now carries body bytes), and storage costs for "hot" replication of full bodies explode. ### The number Peak **read QPS is ~1.4M** (1B users × 40 receives/day, peak factor). Metadata rows at ~1 KB mean ~1.4 GB/sec of inbox-list traffic. If each of those reads pulled the 50 KB body instead, that's **70 GB/sec** — 50× more egress and hot-storage IOPS. ### Trade-off Splitting metadata from body means every message write is now two writes (metadata + body) that can drift out of sync briefly, in exchange for an inbox that stays fast at a billion users.

body.name: Message Body KV
body.summary: Content-addressed KV store holding the full MIME body of each message.

sections.heading: Why separate from metadata
sections.body: Bodies are big (50 KB average, 25 MB max) and read far less often than metadata. Putting them in a cheap KV (Bigtable / RocksDB-backed) keeps the metadata DB lean.

sections.heading: Key
sections.body: `body_id = sha256(user_id || message_id)` — unique per user-copy so deletion is per-user (no cross-tenant leakage on delete).

sections.heading: Compression
sections.body: zstd level 3; typical 3–5x compression on text email. Attachments are NOT stored here — they live in the blob tier referenced by content hash.

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification from per-recipient body copies on large fan-outs
bottlenecks.trigger: Key is sha256(user_id || message_id), so a single inbound message to a 500-person mailing list creates 500 separate body writes into the KV, not one. At 200B msgs/day with ~10% being multi-recipient list traffic, body-write QPS can spike to 3–5x the nominal ~460K inbound msgs/sec, pushing the KV past its concurrency=5000/node budget during bursts.
bottlenecks.symptom: Bigtable/RocksDB tablets serving hot mailing-list bursts show p99 write latency climbing from ~15ms to 100ms+; the Spam→persistence pipeline backs up; MX DATA acks slow down; compaction backlog grows and read p99 follows; storage grows ~Nx faster than expected for list-heavy tenants.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Introduce a two-level key: a shared immutable body stored once under sha256(mime_bytes) (like attachments), plus a tiny per-user pointer row {user_id, message_id → shared_body_hash, refcount}. Dedup collapses N recipients to one ~KB pointer write + one shared body write. Keep per-user delete semantics via refcount GC with 30d grace, identical to the attachment tier.
bottlenecks.detection: Track write-amplification ratio = body_put_qps / distinct_message_ids_per_sec (alert when > 3x sustained 5min), per-tablet write-QPS skew histogram (alert on top-1 > 2% of cluster writes), and compaction pending tasks per node > 50.

bottlenecks.title: Compression CPU saturation on 25MB-max messages
bottlenecks.trigger: Every body write zstd-compresses the MIME payload before PUT. Average 50KB compresses in sub-ms, but the 25MB MIME cap means worst-case compression can burn 200–500ms of CPU per write. At ~460K writes/sec peak across the KV fleet, even 0.1% of messages near the cap (~460/sec) concentrates GB/sec of compression work onto a handful of nodes holding those shards.
bottlenecks.symptom: KV node CPU pegs at 95% on a subset of replicas while peers idle; write p99 climbs from ~15ms to hundreds of ms; upstream API/spam pipeline sees timeouts on the PUT body step; ingestion backlog on the spam filter grows only for messages above ~5MB.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Move compression off the KV hot path: zstd-compress in the API tier (already doing MIME parse) and store pre-compressed bytes, or route messages > 1MB to a dedicated 'heavy' KV pool with higher CPU-to-IOPS ratio. Use zstd level 1 (not 3) for messages > 5MB — 80% of the ratio at 3x the throughput. Stream-compress with a bounded buffer rather than loading full 25MB in RAM.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-node CPU% vs write-QPS scatter plot; `kv_compress_duration_ms` histogram tagged by input_size_bucket with alert at p99 > 100ms; `kv_put_bytes_in / kv_put_bytes_out` ratio to catch compression regressions.

bottlenecks.title: Cold-read tail latency from on-disk bodies during search-result hydration
bottlenecks.trigger: Bodies are read rarely (user opens a message) so they live on cheap disk with minimal cache. But operations that fetch many bodies at once — thread expansion (10–50 messages), 'show original', or re-indexing after schema migration — can issue 50 parallel GETs against cold SSTables. With a 1 PB/day body-storage tier, working set vastly exceeds RAM and reads hit disk nearly every time.
bottlenecks.symptom: Opening a long thread shows visible staggered load as bodies trickle in; p99 body-read latency 60–200ms against a ~15ms target; during bulk re-index jobs, KV read IOPS saturates and user-facing thread opens degrade in parallel; LB/API sees timeout retries on GET /v1/messages/{id}.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Co-locate per-thread bodies on the same tablet by including thread_id in the key prefix (thread_id || user_id || message_id) so a thread open is a single range scan, not 50 random reads. Add a small per-replica LRU for bodies opened in the last 5min (covers reply-chain re-reads). For bulk/backfill jobs, route through a separate read path with its own IOPS budget and rate-limit to < 20% of node capacity.
bottlenecks.detection: `kv_body_read_latency_ms` p99 tagged by access_pattern (single vs thread-batch); cache-hit-ratio gauge (target > 40% for thread opens); alert when bulk-job read QPS > 20% of total or when user-path p99 correlates with backfill job activity.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a separate Message Body KV exists in Gmail-scale mail For a Gmail-style service, every message has two very different parts: a tiny metadata row (sender, subject, labels, ~1 KB) that users scan constantly, and a fat MIME body (50 KB average, up to 25 MB) that users rarely open. If we shoved bodies into the metadata DB, every inbox scroll would drag giant blobs across the wire just to render one-line previews. The Body KV is the "cold lane": cheap, content-addressed, compressed storage that gets touched only when someone actually clicks a message open. ### What breaks without it Collapse bodies back into the metadata DB and Bob's inbox load balloons from a quick metadata scan to dozens of 50 KB fetches per page. The metadata DB's partitions bloat 50× larger, compactions slow, and p99 inbox latency blows past the 50ms target. Operators see Cassandra/Bigtable tablets hot-spotting on big-row reads; users see a spinner every time they open Gmail on mobile. Meanwhile the search indexer's CDC stream now carries body bytes too, pushing index lag past the 5-second freshness target. ### The number At **200B messages/day × 50 KB average body**, that's **10 PB/day raw**, compressed ~3× with zstd to roughly **1 PB/day** of body storage. Compare that to metadata at ~1 KB/msg = **200 GB/day** — bodies are **~5000× heavier than metadata**. Keeping them in separate stores means the hot path (metadata) stays on fast, replicated SSD while the cold path (bodies) lives on cheaper disk-heavy hardware. ### Trade-off Every send is now two writes (metadata + body) that can briefly drift out of sync — accepted in exchange for an inbox that stays fast at a billion users.

blob.name: Attachment Blob Store
blob.summary: Content-addressed S3-style store for attachments, deduplicated across users.

sections.heading: Content addressing
sections.body: Key = `sha256(bytes)`. When 1M users receive the same viral PDF, it's one blob, 1M metadata references. Saves ~3x at Gmail scale.

sections.heading: Access
sections.body: API issues a 10-minute signed URL when the user opens an attachment — bytes flow client → blob directly, not through the API tier.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
sections.body: Reference counted via metadata. When last referring metadata row is deleted + 30d grace → garbage-collect the blob.

gained: Tight integration with in-house GCP infra

bottlenecks.title: Hot-object read storm on viral attachments overwhelming a single blob's placement group
bottlenecks.trigger: Content-addressing means one viral PDF/image (e.g., a company-wide announcement sent to 1M recipients, or a shared newsletter image) is stored as a single blob keyed by sha256(bytes). When recipients open it within a short window, all GETs hit the same key and therefore the same 3-way-replicated placement group. At ~460K reads/sec aggregate and even 0.01% concentrated on one hot object, that single object can see 40K+ GET/sec against a per-object ceiling closer to 1–5K/sec before replica bandwidth saturates.
bottlenecks.symptom: Signed-URL fetches for the hot attachment take seconds instead of 10–60ms; users see 'loading attachment' spinners; placement-group replicas saturate NIC and CPU while rest of fleet is idle; cascading timeouts on the API attachment.exists HEAD path (same hot key) push send latency up for unrelated messages carrying that attachment as a quote.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Detect hot keys online via request-rate sampling and auto-replicate hot objects to a per-region CDN edge tier (CloudFront/Google Cloud CDN) with signed-URL origin; fall back to in-cluster hot-key replication (promote hot blobs from 3x to 20x replicas temporarily); enforce per-client signed-URL rate limits so a runaway client can't hammer one object; serve immutable content-addressed blobs with long Cache-Control (max-age=31536000, immutable) so CDN hit ratio approaches 99%.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-object GET QPS histogram (top-N hot keys dashboard); alert when any single sha256 key exceeds 1000 GET/sec or >1% of cluster read traffic; per-placement-group NIC utilization alert at >70%; CDN origin-hit-ratio gauge (alert when drops below 95% for attachments > 100KB).

bottlenecks.title: Reference-count race conditions causing premature GC or orphaned blobs at 10 PB/day ingest
bottlenecks.trigger: Blobs are reference-counted via metadata rows with a 30d grace, but the metadata DB uses LOCAL_QUORUM writes with eventual consistency to the search index and CDC. At ~460K inbound writes/sec with ~10% carrying attachments (~46K attachment incref ops/sec), concurrent incref/decref during message moves, bulk-delete, and mailing-list fan-out can race: a decref from user A's delete runs before user B's incref is durable, dropping refcount to 0 and scheduling GC of a blob that's about to be referenced again.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rare but catastrophic: users open an old email and get '404 attachment not found' for a blob that was GC'd while still referenced; support escalations with no recovery path since bytes are gone; alternatively, conservative GC leaks blobs and storage grows faster than the 3 PB/day post-dedup estimate (silently paying 2–3x storage bill).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Make refcounts authoritative in a transactional store (Spanner or a dedicated refcount service with CAS), not derived from metadata scans; enforce incref-before-metadata-write ordering in the API tier so blob write + incref is durable before the metadata row commits; implement GC as a two-phase scan (mark + verify after 30d grace + re-verify refcount=0 with a second scan 24h later before delete); keep a tombstone/undelete journal for 90d so accidentally GC'd blobs can be restored from cold archive.
bottlenecks.detection: Counter `blob_gc_resurrection_attempts` (incref on a key currently in pending-GC state) — alert on any non-zero value; periodic reconciliation job comparing sum(metadata.attach_ids refcounts) vs blob.refcount, alert on drift > 0.01%; track `blob_404_on_signed_url` rate (alert at >1 per million).

bottlenecks.title: Signed-URL issuance and verification bottleneck at peak attachment-open QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Every attachment open issues a fresh 10-minute signed URL through the API tier before bytes flow client→blob directly. At ~1.4M peak read QPS with ~10% of messages carrying attachments and users opening ~30% of viewed attachments, peak signed-URL issuance is ~40K/sec. Each URL requires HMAC-SHA256 signing with a rotating key plus a per-user authorization check (does bob actually own a metadata row referencing this sha256?).
bottlenecks.symptom: Attachment-open latency p99 tracks API/metadata latency rather than the blob tier's 10–60ms; during metadata-shard hiccups, attachment opens fan out slowness even though the blob tier is healthy; signing-key rotation events cause brief p99 spikes as caches re-warm.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cache the authorization check per (user_id, sha256) in a replica-local LRU with 5min TTL (same as URL validity) — repeat opens within a session skip the metadata lookup; pre-issue signed URLs in the inbox-list response for visible thumbnails and inline images so the open is zero-RTT; use short-lived but reusable URLs (10min window allows reload without re-signing); move HMAC signing to a native extension or WASM module to keep per-op cost < 50μs; ensure blob store accepts a signature-only verification path with no external calls.
bottlenecks.detection: `signed_url_issue_latency_ms` p99 (alert > 20ms), `signed_url_auth_cache_hit_ratio` (target > 80%, alert < 60%), and correlation dashboard between attachment-open p99 and metadata-DB p99 to catch when blob tier is blamed for upstream slowness.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a dedicated Attachment Blob Store exists in Gmail-scale mail Attachments are fundamentally different from message bodies: they're large (500 KB average, up to 25 MB), frequently duplicated across users (think of a PDF announcement sent to 10,000 employees), and rarely opened after the first view. Stuffing them into the metadata DB or even the body KV would be a disaster — the metadata store is tuned for tiny, fast row reads, and the body KV is already handling 1 PB/day of message text. The blob store is a separate tier specifically designed for large immutable bytes, content-addressed by `sha256(bytes)` so that the viral HR policy PDF gets stored **once** and referenced by a million metadata rows. ### What breaks without it Drop attachments into the body KV and every inbox load that shows an attachment icon risks pulling MBs of PDF bytes through the API tier. The API's 100 replicas — sized for 15ms metadata-shaped work — start holding connections for seconds while proxying binary downloads. LB concurrency saturates, inbox scrolls stall for unrelated users, and storage costs explode because identical attachments get rewritten per recipient instead of deduped. ### The number that forces it Raw attachment ingest is **200B msgs/day × 10% × 500 KB ≈ 10 PB/day**. Content-addressing collapses this to roughly **3 PB/day** — a ~3× savings, or ~2.5 EB/year avoided. At Gmail's storage costs, that dedup alone is the difference between a viable free tier and a bankrupt one. ### Trade-off Reference counting adds operational complexity (the 30-day GC grace window, refcount races on deletion) in exchange for massive storage savings and a clean separation between "message" and "payload."

search.name: Search Index
search.summary: Elasticsearch cluster indexing headers + body text for `search mail` queries.

sections.heading: Index shape
sections.body: One logical index per user, physically grouped into per-shard tenant buckets. Fields: from, to, subject, body, labels, received_at.

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body: Metadata-DB CDC → Kafka → indexer workers → ES bulk API. Lag target < 5 seconds p99.

sections.heading: Query path
sections.body: `GET /v1/messages:search?q=from:alice invoice` → ES query with user_id filter. Typical latency 20–80ms for a single-user query.

sections.heading: Sizing
sections.body: ~5 KB indexed per message. 200B msgs/day * 5 KB ≈ 1 PB/year index on hot hardware; older years archived to warm tier.

bottlenecks.title: Indexer lag blowing the <5s freshness SLO under ingest bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: CDC→Kafka→indexer pipeline must absorb ~460K metadata inserts/sec peak plus ~115K label/flag updates/sec (mark-read, archive, star), each producing a bulk ES doc update. At ~5KB indexed per message and 200B msgs/day, indexer workers face ~1 PB/year of writes; any spike (mailing-list fan-out to 500 recipients = 500 doc inserts for one inbound) or ES bulk-queue backpressure pushes lag past the 5s p99 target.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users send/receive a message, see it in their inbox (metadata DB is authoritative), but searching for it returns nothing for 10–60 seconds; support tickets of 'search is broken', on-call sees Kafka consumer lag climbing and ES `bulk.queue` saturated, indexer worker CPU pegged while ES refresh_interval can't keep up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune ES `refresh_interval` to 1s on hot tenant indices (not the default 30s), use bulk API with 5–10MB batches and 500-doc chunks, scale indexer workers horizontally by Kafka partition (partition key = user_id so ordering is preserved per-user), coalesce label-only updates within a 1s window before emitting to ES, and route large mailing-list fan-outs to a dedicated 'bulk' index pipeline so they don't head-of-line block interactive sends.
bottlenecks.detection: Gauge `search_index_lag_ms` = now - CDC event timestamp at ES commit, alert p99 > 3s for 2min; Kafka consumer lag per partition alert > 100K msgs; ES `bulk.rejected` counter non-zero; `indexer_worker_cpu_pct` > 80% sustained 5min.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-shard skew from power users with millions of indexed messages
bottlenecks.trigger: Per-user logical index grouped into tenant shards, but distribution is Zipfian: a 10-year heavy user (mailing-list subscriber) accumulates 1M+ indexed docs (~5GB at 5KB/doc) while median users have <20K. With retention-forever and 1 PB/year growth, a handful of tenants per shard can push shard size past ES's practical 50GB limit; queries from those users do full BM25 scans over millions of docs.
bottlenecks.symptom: Search latency for long-tenured / high-volume users climbs from the 20–80ms baseline to 500ms–2s, while typical users see fast results; shard-level CPU hotspots on ES data nodes hosting power-user shards, JVM heap pressure and GC pauses, occasional shard-relocation thrash when rebalancing fails to even out byte-sized tenants.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Time-partition indices per user (`mail-{user_id}-{year}`) with ILM rolling hot→warm→cold tiers; route typical queries to the last 2 years only with a 'search older' option that fans out to warm tier; use custom routing by user_id so single-user queries hit exactly one shard; cap hot-shard size at 30GB and rebalance power users onto dedicated shards via shard allocation filtering; force-merge older indices to 1 segment for query efficiency.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard doc count and size histograms, alert when any shard > 40GB or any single user's doc count > 500K; search latency p99 bucketed by user account age and message count; ES `search.query_time_in_millis` per shard with alert on top-1 shard > 3x cluster median.

bottlenecks.title: Expensive wildcard/prefix queries from Gmail-style operators causing thread-pool exhaustion
bottlenecks.trigger: Gmail query grammar allows `from:*@acme.co`, `subject:invoice*`, and substring matches that translate to ES wildcard/prefix queries — these scan term dictionaries instead of using inverted-index lookups. At ~1.4M peak read QPS with even 1% being expensive queries (~14K QPS), each such query can tie up an ES search thread for 100–500ms vs 20ms for exact-term queries.
bottlenecks.symptom: ES `search` thread pool queue builds up, cheap term queries from other users start queuing behind expensive ones, p99 search latency spikes cluster-wide even though average load is normal; circuit breakers trip on fielddata/heap; on-call sees specific users (often corporate or power users with complex filters) correlated with cluster-wide slowdowns.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce query-cost analysis at the API layer before submission: reject queries without at least one selective term, rewrite `from:*@acme.co` into a domain-extracted keyword field (`from_domain: acme.co`) indexed at ingest time so it's a term lookup; cap wildcard/prefix query timeout at 200ms with `search.allow_expensive_queries=false` except on an opt-in slow pool; dedicate a separate ES thread pool / node group for expensive queries so they can't starve the interactive path.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `search_query_duration_ms` p99 tagged by query_type (term, wildcard, prefix, regex); ES `thread_pool.search.queue` alert > 500; `search_rejected` counter non-zero; per-user query-cost histogram to identify abusive patterns and rate-limit at the API tier.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a dedicated Search Index exists in Gmail-scale mail For a Gmail-style service, "search your mail" is a headline feature — users expect to type `from:alice invoice` and get hits across years of messages in under 100ms. The metadata DB is sharded by `user_id` and optimized for one access pattern: "give me the most recent N messages for this user, ordered by time." It has no idea how to find the word *invoice* inside a subject line or body without scanning every row in the partition. A dedicated inverted-index tier (Elasticsearch here) is what makes full-text queries fast: it pre-tokenizes every message at write time so lookups are O(matching docs), not O(all your mail). ### What breaks without it Drop the search index and every search query becomes a full scan of the user's metadata partition plus body KV fetches to grep text. Bob's search for `invoice` across 10 years of mail touches ~180K rows and thousands of body blobs — his query takes 30 seconds, the metadata DB sees massive read amplification, and the body KV (meant to be cold) gets hammered. Operators watch Cassandra p99 collapse cluster-wide because one user's search starves everyone else's inbox scroll. ### The number At **200B messages/day × 5 KB indexed per message ≈ 1 PB/year** of index on hot hardware. That's an entire tier's worth of storage devoted *just* to making text searchable — which is only worth paying for because search latency drops from seconds-to-minutes down to the 20–80ms range. ### Trade-off Search results lag writes by up to 5 seconds (CDC → Kafka → indexer), so a freshly received message may not be findable immediately — accepted in exchange for sub-100ms queries over a petabyte of text.

push.name: Push Notification Service
push.summary: Fan-out service that wakes mobile/web clients when a new message lands.

sections.heading: Triggers
sections.body: Spam filter emits a `new_mail` event after disposition = INBOX; push service dispatches to APNs / FCM / web-push / connected WebSockets.

sections.heading: Why not push everything
sections.body: Bulk / promo mail skips push to protect battery. Only INBOX with importance >= normal triggers a device-level notification.

bottlenecks.title: Device registry fan-out storm during mailing-list blasts
bottlenecks.trigger: A single inbound message to a 10K-recipient mailing list (common at ~460K inbound msgs/sec peak) emits 10K new_mail events, each requiring a device-registry lookup and fan-out to ~3 devices/user = 30K push dispatches from one message. At 1% of inbound being list traffic, that's ~140K push dispatches/sec from list fan-out alone, on top of the baseline ~460K receives/sec × avg 2.5 devices ≈ 1.15M dispatches/sec peak.
bottlenecks.symptom: Push latency p99 climbs from ~40ms to seconds; APNs/FCM rate-limit responses (429s) start appearing; users complain notifications arrive minutes after the inbox already shows the message; device-registry read QPS spikes and co-tenants on that shard see elevated latency.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch device-registry lookups per event (multi-get 100 user_ids per RPC), cache device tokens in a replica-local LRU with 5min TTL keyed by user_id, coalesce events for the same user within a 2s window (one push per user even if 5 list messages arrive), and enforce per-sender event-rate limits upstream at the Spam filter so a single blast can't fan out more than N events/sec into push.
bottlenecks.detection: Gauge `push_events_per_inbound_message` histogram (alert when p99 > 100), `device_registry_lookup_qps` with anomaly detection at 3x baseline, `push_dispatch_lag_ms` p99 > 2s alert, and APNs/FCM `429_rate` > 0.1% sustained 2min.

bottlenecks.title: APNs/FCM upstream rate limits and connection-pool saturation
bottlenecks.trigger: APNs enforces ~1000 concurrent streams per HTTP/2 connection and FCM has per-project QPS quotas. At peak ~1M+ push dispatches/sec across 1B DAU, with serviceTimeMs 10–40ms per provider call, push workers need ~20–40K concurrent in-flight provider requests — exceeding the configured concurrency=5000 per node and requiring careful connection-pool sizing against the providers.
bottlenecks.symptom: Push worker concurrency saturates while CPU is idle (blocked on provider I/O); APNs returns 429 TooManyRequests or resets HTTP/2 streams; FCM returns QUOTA_EXCEEDED; some devices receive notifications while others on the same message don't; on-call sees `push_provider_error_rate` spike during traffic bursts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a pool of persistent HTTP/2 connections to APNs/FCM (≥50 conns/worker to multiply the 1000-stream ceiling), shard push workers by device-token hash so each worker owns a stable subset of connections, implement token-bucket rate limiting per-provider with backpressure to an internal queue, and use exponential backoff with jitter on 429s. For web-push WebSockets, run a separate tier (push is mixed-protocol-unfriendly).
bottlenecks.detection: `push_provider_inflight_requests` per worker (alert at 80% of stream budget), `push_provider_5xx_rate` and `push_provider_429_rate` with alert > 0.5%, per-provider connection-pool utilization gauge, and `push_queue_depth` alert > 10K.

bottlenecks.title: Stale device token accumulation causing wasted dispatches and latency drag
bottlenecks.trigger: With 1B DAU and ~3 devices/user = 3B registered tokens, natural churn (app uninstalls, token rotations, device resets) produces ~1–2% stale tokens/month. Without aggressive cleanup, 5–10% of every fan-out targets dead tokens — at ~1M dispatches/sec peak, that's 50–100K wasted provider calls/sec, each costing a full round-trip before APNs returns Unregistered/BadDeviceToken.
bottlenecks.symptom: Push latency tail grows as workers burn time on dead tokens; APNs/FCM return elevated `Unregistered` feedback; device-registry storage grows faster than active-user count; operators see `push_dispatch_success_rate` slowly decline from 99% to 90% over months; cost of push provider calls inflates without user benefit.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Subscribe to APNs feedback service and FCM's token-invalidation topic; asynchronously decrement/remove tokens returning Unregistered/BadDeviceToken on first failure; TTL tokens to 90 days of inactivity and require client heartbeat to refresh; batch-verify low-activity tokens monthly; dedupe tokens per user_id (a phone that re-registers shouldn't accumulate entries).
bottlenecks.detection: `push_token_invalid_rate` counter by provider (alert > 3%), `device_registry_size / DAU` ratio trend (alert when > 3.5 avg devices/user), `push_dispatch_success_rate` gauge with alert < 95%, and a weekly report of tokens never acknowledged in the last 90 days.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a Push Notification Service sits in this design For a Gmail-style service, "mail arrives" is a *server-side* event — a remote MTA hands a message to our MX, the spam filter scores it, and it lands in Bob's metadata shard. But Bob's phone is asleep in his pocket. Without something actively poking his device, Bob only finds out he got mail the next time he opens the app. The Push service is the bridge between "the message is durably in the inbox DB" and "Bob's lock screen lights up within a second." It subscribes to the `new_mail` event the spam filter emits after disposition=INBOX and fans out to APNs (iOS), FCM (Android), web-push, and any live WebSocket session. ### What happens without it Drop this tier and every client has to *poll* — "any new mail?" every 30 seconds. At 1B DAU that's **~33M polls/sec** hammering the metadata DB, almost all returning "nothing new." The API tier melts, the metadata DB's read replicas saturate on pointless queries, and ironically Bob's battery dies faster from constant radio wake-ups than it would from real push. Operators see inbox-read QPS an order of magnitude above the actual 1.4M peak; users complain notifications are minutes late. ### The number At **1B users × 40 receives/day ≈ 460K new-mail events/sec peak**, with ~2.5 devices/user average, the Push service fans out to roughly **1.15M device dispatches/sec**. Centralizing that fan-out lets us batch device-registry lookups, coalesce multiple messages per user into one notification, and respect APNs/FCM rate limits — none of which a polling client could do. ### Trade-off Accepting a dependency on third-party providers (APNs, FCM) whose outages we can't fix, in exchange for real-time delivery without polling.

operations.title: Send email to an external recipient
operations.name: Send email to an external recipient
operations.description: User clicks Send. API validates, attachments are stored, spam filter scans outbound, MTA delivers via SMTP to the remote domain.

steps.title: User clicks Send
steps.action: Gmail web app serializes the draft as MIME and POSTs it (with references to any previously uploaded attachment blobs) to the submission API.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /v1/messages:send HTTP/1.1
Host: mail.googleapis.com
Authorization: Bearer ya29.a0...
Content-Type: message/rfc822 From: alice@gmail.com
To: bob@example.com
Subject: Q2 invoice
Message-ID: <c7f1-4e2b@gmail.com> --boundary42
Content-Type: text/plain Hi Bob, invoice attached.
--boundary42
Content-Type: application/pdf; name="invoice.pdf"
Content-Disposition: attachment
X-Attach-Ref: sha256:9af3...e21
--boundary42--

steps.title: LB terminates TLS and routes to API
steps.action: L7 LB picks a healthy API replica via least-connections.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.pick(algo="least_conn", healthy=True)
forward(req → upstream)

steps.title: API parses MIME, validates, assigns message id
steps.action: API validates RFC 5322 headers, enforces 25 MB size cap, assigns an internal message_id, and reconciles attachment references against the blob store.
steps.codeOrCommand:
mime = parse_rfc5322(req.body)
if mime.size > 25 * MB: return 413
validate_addresses(mime.headers["From"], mime.headers["To"])
msg_id = uuid7 # time-ordered
for part in mime.attachments: assert blob.exists(part.x_attach_ref) # pre-uploaded via signed URL
envelope = Envelope(msg_id, mime, owner="alice")

steps.title: Spam filter scans outbound for abuse
steps.action: Outbound scan protects sender reputation: checks for phishing patterns, malware attachments, and sending-rate anomalies on the account.
steps.codeOrCommand:
score = classifier.score(mime) # 0.04 (clean)
rate = sender_rate(alice@gmail.com) # 7 msgs/min (ok)
if score > 0.9 or rate > THRESHOLD: return Disposition.QUARANTINE
return Disposition.DELIVER
steps.note: If score were > 0.9 we'd quarantine and notify the sender; > 0.99 silently drops to avoid alerting spammers.

steps.title: API confirms attachment is persisted (already uploaded)
steps.action: Attachment was pre-uploaded via signed URL during composition; API only confirms the content hash exists and increments its reference count.
steps.codeOrCommand:
HEAD /attachments/sha256:9af3...e21
→ 200 OK Content-Length: 182431 ETag: "9af3...e21"
blob.incref("sha256:9af3...e21")

steps.title: API writes message body to KV
steps.action: Full MIME body (minus detached attachments) is compressed and stored under the body key. This is the authoritative body for 'Alice's copy' in Sent.
steps.codeOrCommand:
body_id = sha256("alice" || "01HZ8T7K4C-e4f2")
compressed = zstd.compress(mime_without_attachments) # 12KB → 3.2KB
kv.put(body_id, compressed, durability="quorum")

steps.title: API writes sender's Sent-folder metadata row
steps.action: Single-row insert into Alice's shard of the metadata table, tagged with the SENT label.

steps.title: Outbound MTA connects to remote MX and transmits
